conventions.convention: A real sequence is a function from N to R, indexed starting at 0. Its K-th tail has j-th term x_(j+K).
Convergence and the Cauchy condition use every positive rational ε, identified with its real image. Testing every positive real tolerance is equivalent by rational density.
Eventually means that there exists K such that the property holds for every k ≥ K; frequently means that for every K there exists k ≥ K satisfying the property.
A subsequence uses a strictly increasing map N to N, meaning n_j < n_k whenever j < k.
Boundedness means one real M satisfies |x_k| ≤ M for every index, including the initial block.
Signed-infinity arrows abbreviate eventual inequalities against every real threshold. They do not assert convergence to a real value or license finite-limit algebra.
Natural powers are defined for every real base by a^0 = 1 and a^(k+1) = a^k a; in particular 0^0 = 1. Negative bases in the geometric example use integer powers.
Square root denotes the unique nonnegative root of a nonnegative element of a complete ordered field.

load_bearing.statement: A sequence of reals is a function x : N → R. Boundedness, eventually, frequently, tails and subsequences are defined for these functions; convergence and Cauchyness retain the definition in def-real-limit.

For real sequences x_k → x and y_k → y and real c, sums, scalar multiples, differences and products converge to x+y, cx, x−y and xy. If also y ≠ 0 and y_k ≠ 0 for every k, then 1/y_k → 1/y and x_k/y_k → x/y.
The real sequence x_k := (k+1)^−1 converges to 0, with k+1 the canonical real image of the natural successor. Every term is defined and positive.
Let (x_k) be a sequence of reals converging to x ∈ R. Then there is M ∈ R with |x_k| ≤ M for every k ∈ N.
If a real sequence (x_k) converges to 0 and a real sequence (y_k) is bounded, then (x_k y_k) converges to 0. No convergence assumption is made on (y_k).

If a real sequence (x_k) converges to x and n : N → N is strictly increasing, then (x_(n_k)) converges to x. Consequently, two subsequences converging to different limits imply that the parent sequence does not converge.
For n : N → N, consecutive comparisons n_i < n_(σ(i)) for every i imply strict increase. If n is strictly increasing, then n_k ≥ k for every k ∈ N.
If real sequences satisfy a_k ≤ x_k ≤ b_k eventually and both bounding sequences converge to the same real L, then (x_k) converges to L.

For a real sequence and a real x, convergence to x, convergence of every tail to x and convergence of some tail to x are equivalent. The analogous three Cauchy statements are equivalent. Sequences agreeing eventually therefore have the same convergence-to-x and Cauchy status.
If the same real sequence converges to x ∈ R and to y ∈ R, then x = y.
For a real sequence with x_k > 0 at every index, (x_k) converges to 0 if and only if (1/x_k) diverges to +∞.

The claim that every bounded real sequence converges is false. The recursively defined alternating sequence s_0 = 1, s_(σ(k)) = −s_k is bounded and divergent, with strictly increasing even and odd index maps giving constant subsequences 1 and −1.

seams_checked.note: Checked the supplier page and the relevant definitions and statements against rem-sequence-conventions. Countable means at most countable; the bounded/unbounded subset-of-N classification and pigeonhole exclusion support the equivalence of cofinal and infinite index sets without choice. The finite-list supplier also supports the finite-maxima interpretation.

Checked the supplier page, integer-power definition, power laws, power-sign statement and Bernoulli statement and proof against the geometric example. Natural exponents permit negative bases and 0^0 = 1. Bernoulli is applied with positive h or d, and its equality clause gives equality exactly at k = 0, 1. Root examples use the earlier nonnegative-square-root theorem, which the supplier page explicitly distinguishes from its general nth-root development. No later monotone convergence or rational powers of negative bases are consumed.
